idiom_name: bounded hand-off + capacity signal + explicit full policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: make the consumer's capacity a first-class signal and let the producer wait for it. Between two stages put a buffer with a fixed capacity and an explicit full policy (block the producer, drop oldest/newest, conflate to the latest, or reject); in push APIs the signal is the return value of the send (false/Full/EAGAIN/Pending), in demand-driven APIs it is an explicit request(n)/readiness handshake, and in pull APIs no signal is needed because the consumer only asks when it is ready. Propagate the signal end to end - a stage that buffers without a bound or a producer that ignores the signal turns the pattern into its own failure mode - and treat the bound as a latency budget: with Little's law, bounded queue depth = throughput × target latency.
code_sketch:
queue = bounded_queue(capacity = N, on_full = block | drop_oldest | drop_newest | fail)

# push API: the send tells the producer to wait
if not sink.send(item):            # false / Full / EAGAIN / Pending
    wait_until_ready(sink)         # drain event, await, poll(POLLOUT), ...

# demand API: the consumer declares capacity
subscription.request(n)            # publisher emits at most n more

# pull API: nothing is produced until asked for
for item in source:                # generator / async iterator
    process(item)
pitfalls: An unbounded queue called backpressure: memory grows until the process dies and the producer is never slowed.
A bounded queue with no defined full policy - the behaviour under saturation is then whatever the library happens to do.
Signalling capacity but not propagating it: one unbounded hand-off anywhere in the chain undoes every bound before it.
Blocking waits without a timeout or cancellation, so a stalled consumer becomes a permanently hung producer.

Sizing the buffer for steady-state throughput only: a burst requires proportionally larger headroom or an acceptable shedding policy; a too-small bound converts overload into rejection without providing useful buffering.

Mixing demand-driven (pull) and rate-driven (push) flow control styles in the same pipeline without an explicit translation layer, violating Reactive Streams contracts and creating hidden buffer growth.

Assuming backpressure will cross a boundary the application does not own (external service, managed broker, hardware sensor) instead of adding explicit load shedding or durable buffering at that boundary.
Treating a blocked/stalled stage as a performance bug and removing the bound rather than investigating the downstream bottleneck.

Buffer into an unbounded queue instead of propagating demand -> sustained production above consumption turns backlog into memory exhaustion and latency collapse -> use a finite buffer with an explicit wait, reject, shed or conflate policy.

Request Long.MAX_VALUE/unlimited demand to simplify a consumer -> the publisher is allowed to emit effectively unbounded work and downstream buffers grow -> request finite batches and replenish demand as work completes.

Drop on saturation without declaring or measuring the policy -> callers see success while messages disappear and correctness degrades -> fail/block for lossless work, or count and route deliberate drops for latest-wins/telemetry.
sources: Reactive Streams specification v1.0.4 (reactive-streams.org) - the canonical definition of asynchronous stream processing with non-blocking back pressure: the Subscriber signals demand via Subscription.request(n) and every Publisher must not exceed it, so the queues between threads stay bounded.
Subscription interface (reactive-streams 1.0.0 API) - defines the request(n) and cancel() contract for backpressure signalling between Publisher and Subscriber.
Reactive Streams JVM GitHub repository - TCK, reference implementations, and README detailing the demand-signalling model and recursion/boundedness requirements.
